sources.title: F. Loregian, (Co)end Calculus (arXiv:1501.02503v7)
sources.locator: Chapter 1 'Dinaturality and co/ends', §§1.1-1.4 in full through Example 1.4.5 (printed pp. 2-26, PDF pp. 20-44) AND the chapter Exercises 1.1-1.14 in full (printed pp. 26-30, PDF pp. 44-48); and Chapter 2 §2.2 'Yoneda lemma using co/ends' in full (printed pp. 37-40, PDF pp. 55-58)

contents.name: Definition 1.1.1, dinatural transformation
Remark 1.1.2, dinaturality is naturality on the diagonal of a two-variable functor
Remark 1.1.3, the counit of the cartesian-closed adjunction is dinatural
Definition 1.1.4, co/wedge
Remark 1.1.5, the categories Wd(P) of wedges and Cwd(P) of cowedges
Definition 1.1.6, co/end as a terminal wedge and an initial cowedge
Remark 1.1.7, functoriality of ends under a natural transformation of integrands
Definition 1.1.8, extranatural transformation
contents.reason: Extranaturality is a separate super-naturality notion carrying passive variables, and it is used here for nothing: every wedge and every end on this page is dinatural in the single active variable. Its actual consumer is the enriched functor-category construction, where Kelly's (1.39) needs extranaturality to type the composition morphism.

contents.name: Remark 1.1.9, co/wedges in the extranatural setting
contents.reason: This restates the wedge notion for extranatural families, so it can only be written after extranaturality itself is defined, and it is that definition which is deferred to the enriched development rather than this one.

contents.name: Definition 1.1.10, graphical calculus for extranaturality
contents.reason: A string-diagram calculus for extranatural families; the library has no graphical-calculus formalism and adopting one is a separate development with its own soundness obligations, not a result about ends.

contents.name: Remark 1.1.11, naturality and dinaturality as special cases of extranaturality
contents.reason: The unifying statement is only meaningful once extranaturality is defined, and it subsumes rather than establishes the dinaturality this page uses; it belongs with the extranaturality definition it depends on.

contents.name: Proposition 1.1.12, extranatural transformations are particular dinatural transformations
contents.reason: A comparison theorem between the two super-naturality notions, so it rests entirely on the extranaturality definition deferred above; nothing on this page cites it.

contents.name: Notation 1.1.13, the subscripted and superscripted integral notation for co/ends
Remark 1.1.14, Yoneda's 1960 paper uses the reversed integral notation
Notation 1.1.15, writing the induced arrow as an integral, and functoriality
Remark 1.1.16, Mac Lane on the integration variable being bound
Remark 1.2.1, the arrow-indexed family built from a wedge
Definition 1.2.2, the twisted arrow category tw(C)
Remark 1.2.3, co/ends are co/limits I: wedges correspond to cones over tw(C)
Remark 1.2.4, the equalizer and coequalizer descriptions (1.27) and (1.28)
Remark 1.2.5, a functor promoted as mute in its remaining variable has the same universal property
Definition 1.2.6, preservation and reflection of co/ends
Theorem 1.2.7, every co/continuous functor preserves the co/ends that exist
Corollary 1.2.8, the hom functor commutes with integrals
Remark 1.2.9, the subdivision graph and category of a category
contents.reason: A third index category computing the same end, alongside the twisted arrow category and the equalizer presentation that this page already builds and proves agree. Nothing here or downstream needs the subdivision presentation, and adding it would be a third route to an object already characterised twice.

contents.name: Proposition 1.2.10, the subdivision category is final in tw(C) and computes the same co/end
contents.reason: This is the comparison theorem for the subdivision presentation deferred immediately above, so it cannot be built without that construction; its content is that a third route agrees with the two this page proves agree.

contents.name: Theorem 1.3.1, Fubini theorem for co/ends
Lemma 1.3.2, the cotensor end over the pair variable recovers the end over one variable
contents.reason: This lemma exists to run Loregian's proof of Fubini through an adjoint to the end functor, which requires the target to admit copowers. This page proves Fubini by a universal-property argument that assumes no copowers at all, so the lemma is not a step of any proof written here, while its statement genuinely belongs with the cotensor machinery.

contents.name: Remark 1.3.3, iterated co/ends in any order by induction on the number of variables
Theorem 1.4.1, the set of natural transformations is an end of hom-sets
Remark 1.4.2, Yoneda's closure formulation of naturality for Ab-enriched functors
contents.reason: Stated for functors enriched over abelian groups, so it presupposes a base of enrichment; the enriched notions are a separate development and no ordinary statement on this page is weakened by omitting it.

contents.name: Remark 1.4.3, the end of the hom functor is the monoid of endo-natural transformations of the identity
Example 1.4.4, dinatural transformations between two functors form an end
contents.reason: The construction forms a four-variable Set-valued functor whose end is the collection of dinatural families, and the resulting object is used nowhere on this page; it is a natural companion to the profunctor development, which the library has not planned, so its home is an owner decision rather than an existing page.

contents.name: Example 1.4.5, Stokes' theorem read as a cowedge condition
contents.reason: The cowedge is over the de Rham complex of differential forms on a manifold, so it rests on differential geometry and de Rham cohomology; the exterior derivative and integration of forms are a subject area this page cannot reach.

contents.name: Proposition 2.2.1, the ninja Yoneda lemma, all four co/end isomorphisms
Remark 2.2.2, the name of the ninja Yoneda lemma
Definition 2.2.3, tensor and cotensor in a V-category
Example 2.2.4, a cocomplete locally small category is Set-co/tensored by copies
Remark 2.2.5, tensor, hom and cotensor as a two-variable adjunction
contents.reason: The two-variable adjunction is a structure on a monoidal or enriched base, and neither monoidal structure nor enrichment is available to this page; the ordinary power and copower are defined here directly from their hom-set bijections instead.

contents.name: Remark 2.2.6, the Yoneda embedding read as a Dirac delta
contents.reason: An informal analogy with distribution theory offered explicitly as motivation and not as mathematics; there is no statement here to prove or to cite.

contents.name: Exercises 1.1, deriving the dinaturality equations (1.5) and (1.6) and the diagrams they need
Exercise 1.2, dinatural transformations cannot be composed in general
Exercise 1.2, a dinatural transformation composed with a natural one on either side is again dinatural
Exercise 1.3, the end and the coend of a constant functor
Exercise 1.4, the stalactite, stalagmite and yanking composition rules for extranatural transformations
contents.reason: These three rules are about extranatural transformations, whose definition (1.1.10) this page also declines: extranaturality separates the two mute variables from the dinatural pair and needs the string-diagram calculus to state the yanking rule at all, none of which any item here uses.

contents.name: Exercise 1.5, dinaturality is strictly more general than extranaturality
contents.reason: The separating witness is a dinatural family on the walking arrow that fails extranaturality for a specific choice of mute variable, so the statement cannot even be posed without the extranaturality definition this page declines to build.

contents.name: Exercise 1.6, co/ends valued in a finite product category are computed coordinatewise
contents.reason: The coordinatewise formula for a co/end valued in a finite product category carries the hypothesis that each factor has both an initial and a terminal object, and the exercise itself asks the reader where that hypothesis is used; adopting the result would mean settling a question the source deliberately leaves open.

contents.name: Exercise 1.7, the end of a functor on the walking arrow is a pullback, and dually the coend a pushout
Exercise 1.8, the Elmendorf reconstruction coend and the Galois coend of a field extension
contents.reason: These computations need topological groups acting on spaces, the orbit category of a group and the Galois correspondence for an arbitrary extension; the equivariant-homotopy material behind Elmendorf reconstruction is a subject area the library has not reached.

contents.name: Exercise 1.9, the coequaliser characterisation of a coend dual to Remark 1.2.4
Exercise 1.10, natural transformations as an end read off the equaliser characterisation
Exercise 1.11, the end and the coend of the identity functor on the product category
contents.reason: The co/end of the identity functor on the product category is an object of that product category rather than of the target of an integrand, so it does not instantiate any formula this page proves; it is a curiosity about the shape of the definition and has no consumer here or on the Kan-extension page.

contents.name: Exercise 1.12, restricting a finitely continuous functor to a finitely generating full subcategory preserves the coend
contents.reason: This needs a notion of a full subcategory finitely generating a category, defined through epimorphic factorisations of arrows out of its objects, which the library does not have and which serves generator and presentation theory rather than the end calculus this page builds.

contents.name: Exercise 1.13, an adjunction is equivalent to a natural isomorphism of two ends along the adjoint pair
contents.reason: The forward half would fit here, but the exercise asks for the converse — that the end identity holding naturally in every integrand produces the adjunction — and the Kan-extension page that carries the adjunction-and-end interplay does not scaffold this characterisation either, so it has no planned home.

contents.name: Exercise 1.14, a second proof of the Fubini theorem through the copower adjunction
contents.reason: This is the copower-and-adjoint route to Fubini, which requires the target to have the copowers that the Fubini theorem scaffolded here deliberately does not assume; adopting it would narrow the theorem this page proves rather than enrich it.

contents.name: Proposition 3.5.1, iterated limits and colimits over a product index category
Lemma 3.5.2, the canonical interchange morphism from a colimit of limits to a limit of colimits
contents.reason: The comparison map between a colimit of limits and a limit of colimits is about mixing the two kinds of universal object, whereas every interchange this page needs is limit with limit; the mixed comparison and the conditions making it invertible belong with filtered-colimit technology rather than with ends.

contents.name: Examples 3.5.3, the interchange morphism is not an isomorphism in general
contents.reason: These witnesses refute invertibility of the mixed interchange morphism of Lemma 3.5.2, so they cannot be stated without that morphism, which is itself deferred above.

contents.name: Exercise 3.5.4, find a concrete counterexample to the interchange morphism being invertible
contents.reason: An exercise asking the reader to complete the witness of Examples 3.5.3, which is itself about the mixed interchange morphism this page does not build.

sources.locator: §2.1 'Ends in V' in full (printed pp. 27-29, PDF pp. 33-35); §3.1 'Indexing types; limits and colimits; Yoneda isomorphisms' in full (printed pp. 37-39, PDF pp. 43-45); §3.4 'The connexion with classical conical limits when V = Set' in full (printed pp. 42-44, PDF pp. 48-50); §3.7 'Tensor and cotensor products' in full (printed pp. 48-49, PDF pp. 54-55); §3.9 'The inadequacy of conical limits' in full (printed pp. 50-52, PDF pp. 56-58). (3.8), the two representations rewritten as indexed limits in the base
(3.9), the indexed colimit of base-valued functors is symmetric in weight and diagram
contents.reason: This symmetry is special to a base-valued diagram and its use in Kelly is to derive the canonical expression of a functor as a colimit of representables, which is the density theorem; that theorem and the free-cocompletion development it serves are the next page's subject and it is the page that needs this symmetry.

contents.name: (3.10), the Yoneda isomorphisms for a representable weight
(3.11), the limit and colimit bifunctors on pairs for which the object exists
contents.reason: Assembling weighted limits into a bifunctor of weight and diagram selects a representing object for every pair in a proper class, which this library states only in data-supplied form; the honest bifunctor statement therefore needs the chosen-object machinery that the Kan extension page builds when it assembles pointwise extensions into a functor.

contents.name: (3.12), the Yoneda isomorphisms are natural in the object and the diagram
contents.reason: The naturality statement is about the bifunctor of (3.11), so it cannot be stated before that assembly is available, and the same data-supplied treatment applies.

contents.name: (3.24), cones with a given vertex correspond to cones over the hom-functor with vertex a one-point set
(3.25), the classical conical limit and colimit as representations
(3.26), the classical limit is the limit indexed by the constant one-point functor
(3.27), the counit of the constant-weight limit is the limit cone
(3.28), a limit of a set-valued functor is its set of cones with one-point vertex
(3.29), representables carry conical limits to limits of hom-sets
(3.30), the limit over the category of elements of a weight is the set of natural transformations from it
(3.31), the canonical inductive cone of representables over the category of elements
contents.reason: This cone is the data of the density theorem: it presents an arbitrary set-valued functor as a colimit of representables. Density and the free cocompletion are the subject of the following page, which states the cone and proves it is colimiting.

contents.name: (3.32), every set-valued functor is the canonical colimit of representables
contents.reason: This is the density theorem itself. Its proof needs the colimit-of-representables cone of (3.31) and the symmetry (3.9), and the page that develops density and the free cocompletion is where both land.

contents.name: (3.33), an indexed limit is the conical limit over the category of elements of the weight
(3.34), an indexed colimit is the conical colimit over the opposite category of elements
(3.35), the colimit of a set-valued functor is the set of connected components of its category of elements
§3.4 closing remarks on conservative and faithful ordinary functors, and extremal epimorphic counits
contents.reason: These are statements about adjunctions and factorisation properties of functors, placed at the end of the section for later use in Kelly's density chapter; they mention no limit weight and nothing on this page cites them, while conservativity and adjunction machinery already sit on the published adjunction pages.

contents.name: (3.42), the defining bijection of the cotensor product
(3.43), the counit of a cotensor product
(3.44), the defining bijection of the tensor product
§3.7, when the base is Set the cotensor is the power and the tensor is the copower
(3.45) and the two-object 2-category witness, the underlying bijection does not detect a cotensor
contents.reason: The witness is a 2-category, so the base of enrichment is Cat and the point is that an enriched universal property is strictly stronger than its underlying one; with a Set base the two coincide and there is nothing here to state.

contents.name: Proposition 3.46, a V-category is cotensored when its underlying category is complete, for conservative V
contents.reason: The hypotheses quantify over objects of a base of enrichment and over its extremal-epimorphic quotients, so the statement has no content until enrichment is defined.

contents.name: (3.47), the continuity of an indexed limit in its index, extended by cotensors
contents.reason: The three-term identity relates an indexed limit whose index is itself an indexed colimit, and it is stated for a cotensored V-category; the ordinary consequences this page needs are obtained directly from the end formula instead.

contents.name: (3.48), the cocontinuity of an indexed colimit in its index, extended by tensors
contents.reason: The dual three-term identity, stated for a tensored V-category and used in Kelly to run the enriched Kan extension calculus; it belongs with the enriched limit development.

contents.name: §3.9, the comparison map (3.56) from the conical colimit over the category of elements of a weight to that weight
§3.9, (3.56) is not an isomorphism in general, and fails already for V = Ab even though Ab is conservative
§3.9, there is in general no V-functor constant at an object, so the notion of a cone does not enrich
(3.57) and (3.58), the conical limit of a V-functor defined as the limit weighted by the constant unit, for cartesian closed V
contents.reason: This is the enriched form of the constant-weight comparison this page proves in the unenriched case; stating it needs a cartesian closed base and the V-functor category, both of which the enriched-categories page mints and this page deliberately does not.

contents.name: §3.9, when V is conservative every object lies in the closure of the unit under small colimits, so conical completeness still yields all indexed limits
contents.reason: The closure of the unit under small colimits, and the conservativity of the underlying-object functor, are properties of the base of enrichment; neither can be stated on a page whose weights are Set-valued and whose base is not a variable.

contents.name: §3.9, (3.56) is an isomorphism whenever the weight is left exact, for many bases including Cat and Gpd
contents.reason: Left exactness of a V-functor and the enriched universal algebra this observation serves rest on finitely complete bases of enrichment and enriched algebraic theories, a subject area the library has not reached at any order.

contents.reason: The formula is the definition of a pointwise right Kan extension, an object this page does not introduce; the page that defines local and global Kan extensions is where the weighted description is stated and proved.

contents.reason: This identifies presheaves with a class of functors characterised by a unique-lifting property, which needs the notion of a discrete fibration; the fibration language serves the Grothendieck-construction development rather than any weighted limit computed here.

contents.name: Example 7.1.10, the category of simplices of a simplicial set
contents.reason: Simplicial sets and the simplex category are a homotopy-theoretic development the library has not reached, so the example has no objects to name.

contents.name: Example 7.1.11, the category of elements of a hom-weight is a slice category
contents.reason: The identification is stated for the weight that computes a pointwise Kan extension, and its purpose is the comma-category formula for that extension; it lands with the Kan extension page that states the formula.

contents.reason: A statement about the simplex category, which the library has not built; nothing on this page refers to simplicial objects.
